newsitem.title: INDIA: India's oil trouble bubbles as coalition frets.
newsitem.headline: India's oil trouble bubbles as coalition frets.

text.p: Taking a hard decision like raising petroleum prices does not come easy in the world's largest democracy, and on Monday India's policy-makers left the oil trouble bubbling as coalition politics got in the way again.

The United Front (UF) government's steering committee has already met twice and failed to find a way to whittle down a $4.9-billion debt to oil companies, owed for selling petroleum products below market prices to support India's subsidy regime.
"The oil sector is so politically sensitive we cannot apply the general rule that economic reforms have become depoliticised in India," Tridib Pathak, at UBS Securities Pvt Ltd, told Reuters.
A third attempt to find a way to repay the companies was set for Tuesday, but called off as the 15-member coalition grappled with yet another crisis.
"The steering committee meeting has been deferred," a UF official told Reuters.
He gave neither a reason for the postponement, which is the third deferral, nor a new date for the meeting.
But the Press Trust of India pinned the blame on the coalition's internal politics following a split in the Janata Dal party, to which Prime Minister Inder Kumar Gujral belongs.
PTI said leftist members of the coalition plus remaining members of the rump Janata Dal had reservations about the continued presence in the UF of former Janata Dal leader Laloo Prasad Yadav.
The breakaway faction of the Janata Dal, led by Laloo Yadav, has pledged support for Gujral, but it is one more fissure in the centre-left coalition.
Gujral's government is safe for now, propped up by Congress.
But no party inside or outside Gujral's coalition wants to burn potential votes by favouring a price rise when an election could come at any time.
The main opposition Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) and Congress, the second largest party, have both come out against price rises.
And inside the coalition, the leftist parties have remained staunchly opposed to any increase that would hit India's poor.
"I've stopped taking bets on oil prices," said Subra Subramaniam, chief analyst at ABN AMRO Hoare Govett in Bombay, adding that politics would play the deciding role.
Subramaniam said any decision on oil prices may depend on whether Gujral gives ground to his allies on the left, given the split in his own party.
Shrivatsa Kumar, analyst at Jardine Fleming (India) Broking said action was needed urgently as oil companies faced a payments crunch for crude needed to keep refineries running.
"The government must take a bold step, and the sooner the better," Kumar said.
Some analysts expect the government to settle on a petroleum product price rise of less than 10 percent and a mix of other measures, including lower import tariffs for crude and products.
"There will be a single digit price hike in petrol, diesel and kerosene, and other industrial inputs like naptha and fuel oil," said P. Dhileepan, an oil analyst at NatWest Markets in Bombay.
"I don't think consumers will mind very much," he said.
Dhileepan estimated the deficit was currently around 175 billion rupees, up from 155 billion on March 31, the end of 1996/97 fiscal year.
Kumar believed an average price rise of 12-15 percent was needed, and anything less would leave the industry ill-prepared for deregulation and privatisation.
